_comment: Language-neutral parity fixtures: each runs in BOTH the JS engine and ancir_runtime.py; outputs/results are compared within tolerance. The JS emitter is the single source of input DATA: 'generate' specs (seeded rhythm/groups/linear) are realised in JS and written into js_results.json so Python analyses identical arrays. Column refs in args use '@ref' tokens. tableProcess outputs compare by CANONICAL key (trailing _<id> stripped: cosinory_13 -> cosinory). tableProcessResult compares named fields of the single comparison. Add a fixture = add an entry. See tools/README-parity.md.

fixtures.note: NPCRA on a NUMBER x (hourly from 0) with the FIRST and LAST times missing. computeNPCRA kept every row whose Number(t) is finite, and Number(null) is 0, so both rows became samples at hour 0: the epoch grid started an hour early and their y values were averaged into the first epoch. A missing time is now dropped (isInvalidValue), which the Python and R ports already did.

A correlogram of a BinnedData output on a TIME input: 1 h bins stepping 0.5 h (diffStep), so the x column's binWidth (1) is twice its spacing. The app takes the lag step from the column's binWidth; the Python export estimated it from the spacing (0.5).
An imported 'bin' column (binWidth 0.75 h on a 0.5 h step, as the Enspire wells schema creates). The app's lag step is the binWidth, 0.75; the Python export used the spacing, 0.5.

A plain NUMBER x starting at 5 h whose spacing cycles 1, 1, 1.05 h (within 10% of the median, so the index-shift path). The app's lag step is the MEAN spacing, (last - first) / (n - 1) = 1.0167 h, over hoursSinceStart; the Python export used the median, 1 h, over the raw x (the offset itself changes nothing: the autocorrelation is shift-invariant).

Two series. The first is a TIME x whose spacing alternates 0.25 and 0.75 h (not uniform, so the time-pair path), with maxLag 30 h and minLag 2 h saved on the SERIES as the app saves them; the app's lag step is the mean spacing, 0.5 h, where the Python export used the median (0.25 h) and read plot-level corrMaxLag / corrMinLag keys the app never writes. The second is a regular hourly time series on the auto lag range.

Two series whose x has a missing END, no binWidth, so the lag step is the mean spacing. The first is a NUMBER x from 5 h, hourly, with the LAST time missing; the second a TIME x every 0.5 h with the FIRST time missing. The app used (t[n-1] - t[0]) / (n-1) over the raw rows and read the missing end as 0: the first series got a step of about -5/(n-1), negative, so the plot was blank, and the second a step of 0.5 * (n-2)/(n-1), so every lag was mislabelled. The step is (t_j - t_i) / (j - i) over the first and last VALID rows (utils/correlogram.js meanSpacing), which the Python port already used; it equals the old formula whenever both ends are present.

computeAutocorrelation with no binSize (how RhythmicityAnalysis and MovingAnalysis call it) on spacings 1,1,1,2,2,2: the app's step is the UPPER median, the element at floor(len / 2) of the sorted spacings (2), not the mean of the middle two (1.5, what np.median and R's median give), so the lags are 2 and 4 h, not 1.5, 3 and 4.5 h. Its lag slots were also the old overlapping ones: three pairs exactly 1 h apart (half the 2 h step) were counted at lag 0 AND at lag 2, and two pairs 3 h apart at lag 2 AND lag 4, and lag 0 left out each sample's pairing with itself, so it read -0.142 instead of 1. With lag 0 defined as 1 and half-open slots [(k - 1/2) dt, (k + 1/2) dt) (utils/correlogram.js), the correlations are 1, 0.0423, -0.0941 (were -0.142, -0.140, -0.331).

Pairs exactly on a lag-slot boundary. Uneven times (the time-pair path) with the step given as 1 h and minLag 1 h (so lag 0 is out of it): many separations are exactly 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 ... h, half-way between two lags. Slots are half-open, lag k takes (k - 1/2) dt <= d < (k + 1/2) dt, so each such pair is counted once, in the UPPER lag. The old window |d - k dt| <= dt / 2 counted it in both.

Distinct samples closer than half a step. Uneven times with four near-coincident pairs (0.1, 0.2, 0.05 and 0.3 h apart) and a 1 h step. Lag 0 is exactly 1 by definition; the near-zero pairs estimate the correlation at a small NON-zero lag, so they are not used at any lag (they are below the lag-1 slot). The old code excluded each sample's pairing with itself and averaged only the near-zero pairs, so lag 0 was their correlation, not 1.

Two series starting on different days, the second with a leading gap and a coarser step. The app folds BOTH at the earliest valid sample over all series, snapped to that day's midnight (4 March), so series 1's first bar lands in period 2, not period 1 of its own day.

Display zone America/New_York: the first sample (03:40Z on 8 March) is 22:40 on 7 March there, so rows start at New York midnight on 7 March (05:00Z), not UTC midnight on 8 March. The record crosses the 10 March DST change, which must not move the rows.
One series in UTC whose first sample is 06:20, not midnight, on a 0.3 h step that never lands on a row boundary, so every row's first and last bar is split at the boundary.
A number x axis starting at 5 h with 23.5 h rows: bars sit at the raw x (no start-of-day snap), split at multiples of 23.5.

A BinnedData node's output on a TIME input starting at midnight: the output is a time column of bin STARTS (epoch ms) carrying binWidth = binSize and originTime_ms = the input's first sample. binSize 1.5 h, so rows split bars at 0, 1.5, 3, ... and a bar straddles no boundary; the day boundary 24 h is a multiple.
The same on an input whose first sample (the output's originTime_ms) is 06:20Z, in the America/New_York display zone: bars start at 06:20Z = 01:20 New York, 1.333 h into row 1, and are 1 h wide.

A BinnedData node's output on a NUMBER input starting at 5 h: a 'bin' column whose raw values are bin starts (5, 6, 7, ...) and whose getData is the centres. The actogram places bars at the raw starts, not the centres.

An imported 'bin' column (as the Enspire multiplate wells schema creates) carrying binWidth 0.75 h on a 0.5 h step (so the bars are the column's binWidth wide, not the scanned step) and originTime_ms at 07:30Z, plotted with a time series whose first sample is 02:00Z. Its bars shift by the origin's time of day: raw start 0 lands at 7.5 h in row 1.

Pins the cross-language cleaning rule for blank cells: '' and whitespace-only strings are MISSING data (skipped), never coerced to 0; the genuine 0 and the numeric string '3' are data. Python's float('') raises and R's as.numeric(' ') is NA, so both always treated blanks as absent - isNaN('')===false made JS the outlier until isInvalidValue closed the hole. Valid values are [5, 0, 7, 3, 2]: n=5, mean=3.4.

fixtures.rToleranceWhy: R's shapiro.test and the JS port both implement Royston AS R94 and agree on W to 2.8e-11; only the p-value's normalising transform differs, by 5.4e-8. That is a tail-approximation coefficient difference, not a disagreement about the statistic, so R is held to 1e-6 here while Python stays at the default.

fixtures.note: Pins utils/qq.js qqPoints (Blom positions + Acklam quantile + quartile line + pointwise envelope) against scipy. scipy.stats.probplot defaults to Filliben positions, NOT Blom, so the Python side computes the positions explicitly — norm.ppf((arange(1,n+1)-0.375)/(n+0.25)) — matching the JS (and the Shapiro-Wilk m-value convention). Quartiles use np.quantile's default linear (type-7) interpolation, matching describeStats and utils/qq.js. The R side is a genuine third opinion: qnorm/dnorm rather than Acklam or ndtri, with the same explicit Blom positions (R's own ppoints() drops the 3/8 constant above n = 10) and quantile(type = 7). rTolerance 1e-6 (same order as the other Acklam-vs-exact fixtures, e.g. util-normality-shapiro): JS's normalQuantile is only accurate to ~1.15e-9, and dividing by dnorm(z) in the band SE amplifies that to ~1e-8 absolute in bandLo/bandHi — R's exact qnorm and scipy's exact ndtri agree with EACH OTHER far tighter than either does with JS's approximation, which is the expected shape of this disagreement, not a bug.

Pins the probability-plot correlation r the Q-Q plot displays (utils/qq.js qqCorrelation, also its qq_r metric column) against scipy.stats.pearsonr of the sorted sample vs norm.ppf at the same BLOM positions the plot draws. Filliben's original statistic uses Filliben positions; Blom is deliberate, matching the drawn quantiles (see util-qq-points-normal). Same 16-value input (one null) as that fixture, so n also pins the clean-count.

fixtures._comment: Peak-of-the-correlogram convention, checked in all three languages. X is a triangle wave of period 8 correlated with ITSELF, so r is exactly +1 at lag 0 and exactly -1 at lags -4 and +4. A sign-blind argmax that keeps the first winner reports lag -4 with r = -1; the peak must be lag 0 with r = +1.

The peak of an AUTOcorrelogram is the dominant PERIOD, which is a different question from the cross-correlogram's peak and needs a different rule. The input is a triangle wave of period 6 sampled 40 times. Lag 0 is exactly 1 by definition, so an argmax over every lag answers 0 and says nothing (what the Python and R ports did). The repeats at 12 and 18 are normalised by ever fewer overlapping pairs and come out ABOVE the one at 6, so an argmax that merely skips lag 0 answers 18 (what the JS did). The peak is the largest correlation in the first positive lobe: lag 6.

fixtures.note: A NUMBER x (hourly from 0) whose LAST time is missing. The node coerced its times with Number, so the missing row went into the FFT at t = 0: the FFT's own step came out negative, it returned an empty spectrum and the observed statistic was 0. The same coercion made the hours-to-samples step for the block bootstrap (t[n-1] - t[0]) / (n-1) read the end as 0. The node now keeps the rows where x and y are both present (as both ports always did) and takes the step from the first and last present times (utils/validPairs.js meanSpacing, shared with the Correlogram). Only `observed` is compared: the p-value is Monte Carlo (see Known boundaries).

A TIME x (every hour from 2024-03-04T00:00Z) whose FIRST timestamp is missing. hoursSinceStart keeps it as null and starts the rest at 0, so the old Number coercion put the missing row at t = 0 beside the real first sample and its y went into the FFT. The observed statistic is now computed on the present (x, y) rows only, as in both ports.
oddsRatio is Infinity here; JSON cannot represent it, so only the p-value is compared. The Infinity case is covered by the JS unit test.

fixtures.rToleranceWhy: Same cause as util-normality-shapiro: R's shapiro.test and the JS port both implement Royston AS R94 and agree on W, but the p-value's normalising transform differs in the 8th significant figure. Surfaces here because the analysis reports the p-value. Python stays at the default tolerance.

R fits with glm(family = binomial), an independent IRLS from the JS and statsmodels ones. Coefficients and odds ratios agree exactly; the standard errors, built from the final iteration's weights, differ by ~5e-9 once glm's epsilon is tightened to 1e-12 (at its 1e-8 default the gap is ~5e-5). That is the convergence limit of two separate implementations, not a formula disagreement. Python stays at the default tolerance.

Nonlinear fit: R reaches the optimum with optim(L-BFGS-B) + an analytic Jacobian, scipy with trust-region least_squares. They agree to ~1e-8 on the fitted parameters, which is inside 1e-6 but not the 1e-9 default.

fixtures._comment: Free period inside an explicit range (20 to 28 h). Pins the bounded optimiser, the periodogram-seeded start and the acrophase (time of peak) convention for free fits in all three languages.
fixtures.rToleranceWhy: Nonlinear fit: R uses optim(L-BFGS-B), scipy trust-region least_squares, JS Levenberg-Marquardt; all reach the same bounded optimum to ~1e-8.

fixtures._comment: A weak 24 h rhythm on a strong linear trend with the default 1 to 48 h range. Unbounded, the free fit followed the trend out of the circadian range; now every language stops on the 48 h bound (and the JS node warns).
Short (1.4 cycle) fixed-period record, where cov(beta, gamma) is not negligible: pins the delta-method amplitude CI (full covariance) and the time-of-peak acrophase CI, JS vs Python.

fixtures.note: BinnedData on a TIME input (first sample 06:20Z). The app's x output is a time column of bin STARTS in epoch ms (origin + start hours), which getData returns unchanged. The ports used to write bin-centre HOURS into a time column, read back as milliseconds.

The app's saved arg names: aggFunction (not aggFunc) picks the aggregate, and stepSize (default 0.25) is only used when diffStep is true, otherwise the step is binSize. Here aggFunction 'max', binSize 2, stepSize 0.25, diffStep false: 2 h bins on a 2 h step, max of each.

diffStep TRUE: overlapping 3 h windows stepping by stepSize 1 h, median of each. The app's headless compute (definition.func, used by this emitter, the MCP engine and the demo generator) used to ignore diffStep and step by binSize, so it disagreed with the node's own panel; both now read the step from args through one rule.

Custom-edge (cuts) bins on a NUMBER input, aggFunction 'mean'. Edges saved unsorted with a duplicate ([10,0,1,2.5,3,3.2,7,1] -> 0,1,2.5,3,3.2,7,10, uneven). The app's rules (wrangleData.js binData): every bin is [a,b) except the last, which is [a,b] (10 is kept); a value within 1e-10 below an edge belongs to the NEXT bin (0.99999999999 falls in [1,2.5)); values outside the edges (-1, 12) are dropped; [3,3.2) is empty; x is sorted first. (Missing x and y are pinned by the tp-binneddata-missing-* fixtures.) The x output is the bin STARTS read back unchanged (binWidth null).

The app's rules (wrangleData.js binData): every bin is [a,b) except the last, which is [a,b] (10 is kept); a value within 1e-10 below an edge belongs to the NEXT bin (0.99999999999 falls in [1,2.5)); values outside the edges (-1, 12) are dropped; [3,3.2) is empty; x is sorted first. Cuts mode on a TIME input. The app refuses it (BinnedData.svelte: custom cuts are not allowed for a time x) and returns invalid without writing outputs; the ports must refuse it too rather than bin the hours since start.
Cuts mode with fewer than two distinct edges after sort and dedupe ([4,4] -> [4]): the app returns invalid and writes nothing.

Uniform bins (2.5 wide from 0) on the same irregular input, aggFunction 'stddev'. The app's stddev is the SAMPLE standard deviation (n - 1) and 0 for a bin of fewer than two points; its count is the number of pairs in the bin (0 when empty). The ports used the population stddev and had no count (it fell through to the mean).

Uniform bins (2.5 wide from 0) on the same irregular input, aggFunction 'count'. The app's stddev is the SAMPLE standard deviation (n - 1) and 0 for a bin of fewer than two points; its count is the number of pairs in the bin (0 when empty). The ports used the population stddev and had no count (it fell through to the mean).

Missing values in BOTH x and y: x is null at rows 4 and 11, y at rows 3 and 10. A row with a missing x or y is DROPPED, never binned as 0. The app's binData used to filter pairs with the global isFinite, and isFinite(null) is true, so a null y was averaged in as 0 (and became the bin min, reported as null) and a null x put its y in the bin at 0; the Python and R ports already dropped them. Uniform 2.5-wide bins from 0, mean: bin [0,2.5) holds y 2, 8, 12, 11 (mean 8.25) and bin [7.5,10), whose only row has a null y, is empty. The pre-fix app averaged the null y in as 0 and binned the two null-x rows (y 6 and 60) at x = 0, giving 99/7 = 14.14, and reported the empty bin as 0.

Missing values in BOTH x and y: x is null at rows 4 and 11, y at rows 3 and 10. A row with a missing x or y is DROPPED, never binned as 0. The app's binData used to filter pairs with the global isFinite, and isFinite(null) is true, so a null y was averaged in as 0 (and became the bin min, reported as null) and a null x put its y in the bin at 0; the Python and R ports already dropped them. Uniform 2.5-wide bins from 0, min: bin [0,2.5) has min 2; the pre-fix app reported null (its min kept the null y and returned it).

Missing values in BOTH x and y: x is null at rows 4 and 11, y at rows 3 and 10. A row with a missing x or y is DROPPED, never binned as 0. The app's binData used to filter pairs with the global isFinite, and isFinite(null) is true, so a null y was averaged in as 0 (and became the bin min, reported as null) and a null x put its y in the bin at 0; the Python and R ports already dropped them. Custom edges saved with a missing edge ([10,1,null,2.5,7] -> 1,2.5,7,10; the pre-fix app read the null as an extra edge at 0), mean: [1,2.5) holds 8, 12, 11; [7,10] holds 40 and 70 (the null-y row at x = 8 is dropped, where the pre-fix app averaged it in as 0).

Missing values in BOTH x and y: x is null at rows 4 and 11, y at rows 3 and 10. A row with a missing x or y is DROPPED, never binned as 0. The app's binData used to filter pairs with the global isFinite, and isFinite(null) is true, so a null y was averaged in as 0 (and became the bin min, reported as null) and a null x put its y in the bin at 0; the Python and R ports already dropped them. Custom edges saved with a missing edge ([10,1,null,2.5,7] -> 1,2.5,7,10; the pre-fix app read the null as an extra edge at 0), count: the number of COMPLETE pairs in each bin (3, 4, 2).

Fisher's exact (testType 'fisher') on two PAIRED category columns (the demo-workflow-stats-fisher-exact data): p, df NaN, statistic NaN, effect size = the conditional-MLE odds ratio, ciLow/ciHigh its exact 95% interval. Neither port had a Fisher mode: both ran the chi-squared independence test instead.
Fisher's exact, alternative 'greater', same paired data. The p-value is one-sided; the app's interval stays the two-sided 95% one.

Independence on two INDEPENDENT GROUPS (the demo-workflow-stats-two-groups-counts data: 7 of 10 vs 2 of 25), with NO dataFormat saved, so the app's default 'groups' applies: each column is one group's outcomes, tabulated group x outcome (groupsToTable). Both ports cross-tabulated the columns row by row as if paired.
Fisher's exact on the same two independent groups (dataFormat 'groups').

Goodness of fit (the app's testType is 'goodness'; the ports only knew 'goodnessoffit') on a CATEGORY column: tabulated by first appearance, a missing cell and the string 'NaN' skipped, tested against a uniform expectation; effect size Cohen's w.
Goodness of fit on a NUMBER column read as observed counts (a missing cell dropped, not counted as 0).

Correlation, method 'auto', on the demo-tp-correlation data. The app picks ONE method for the whole matrix by Jarque-Bera (n >= 8, sample-SD moments, p >= 0.05 is normal): all three columns pass, so Pearson (input 2 is an exact linear map of input 1, r = 1). Both ports ran Shapiro-Wilk per PAIR, which rejected the cosine-shaped columns and gave Spearman (r = 0.9994).

Correlation, method 'auto', where ONE of three columns is strongly skewed (Jarque-Bera rejects it): the app switches the WHOLE matrix to Spearman, including the pair of the two normal-looking columns, which a per-pair rule would have left on Pearson.

Correlation 'auto' where the choice hinges on HOW the app's Jarque-Bera standardises. Column c (n = 10, right-skewed) has JB p = 0.086 with the SAMPLE standard deviation the app uses, so every column passes and the matrix is Pearson; with the population SD (the NormalityTest node's convention) its p would be 0.016 and the matrix would switch to Spearman.
Independence on the paired demo data WITHOUT Yates' continuity correction (correction false): the uncorrected statistic and its p; Cramer's V is the uncorrected one either way.
Fisher's exact, alternative 'less' (the lower tail, P(X <= a)), same paired data.

fixtures.toleranceWhy: Both ports now run the app's own multi-start Levenberg-Marquardt (rectwave.js fitWithLM) rather than scipy/optim, so they land on the same optimum as the JS: Python agrees to 1e-10; R (vectorised normal equations, BLAS summation order) to within 1e-6. The model's flat, saturating surface was the reason for the old 1e-3, which only an independent optimiser needed.

Both ports now run the app's own Levenberg-Marquardt in the (t1, u, T) coordinates (doublelogistic.js fitWithLM), so the fitted curve itself is compared pointwise, not only the fit quality. The old 1e-3 covered independent optimisers (scipy, optim) landing a sub-1% shift apart on the near-vertical edges.

fixtures._comment: RemoveTrend happy path (index x axis, linear model) — the detrend maths itself was never parity-pinned before the refusal work touched all three runtimes.
Refuse-and-pass-through: the logarithmic model needs x > 0, and the index axis starts at 0 — all three runtimes must return the input UNCHANGED (not an all-NaN column).

fixtures.note: Hourly data at 1 h bins (one point per bin), so the ports' mod-binning fold equals the JS binData-then-fold pipeline. Pins the distinct-fold period axis (18..30 h at 1 h spacing for a 0.05 h step) and the power at each fold through the node.
Enright through the Rhythmicity Analysis node, with a 40 h gap (null y) that leaves empty bins. Pins the distinct-fold period axis and the Enright power at each fold.

binSize equals the 1 h sampling interval, so every bin holds exactly one point and the Python/R mod-binning fold IS the JS binData-then-fold pipeline: period, power, effective df AND threshold must agree exactly. Powers and df were unpinned before the occupancy-weighted empty-bin fix; only the threshold was compared.

The empty-bin regime: 0.25 h bins on HOURLY data leave 3 of every 4 bins permanently empty (the app's default binSize is 0.25 h, so this is the demo-default configuration). Pins the occupancy-weighted Sokolove-Bushell Qp with effective df = occupied-fold-columns - 1 across all three languages — the pre-fix code counted empty bins in the normalisation (Qp inflated ~2.5-10x above its chi-square null on pure noise) and in df (95 instead of 23 at period 24), so statistic, threshold and p disagreed with each other. At period 24 this fixture's power/df/threshold must equal the binSize-1 fixture's values at period 24 exactly (empty bins carry no information).

A 0.05 h step at 1 h bins: 241 trial periods but only 13 distinct folds. Each language must return one point per fold at the period it actually tests (18, 19, ..., 30 h; not the first trial period of each fold, which biased the peak by -binSize/2), and the Sidak family size must be the 13 folds, not the 241 trial periods.

Hourly data at 1 h bins. Pins the app's Enright statistic in every language: for each distinct fold, the mean lag-product correlation over every multiple of the fold, over the binned variance. The Python/R ports used to compute a single-lag normalised autocorrelation, a different statistic.

15 min data at 1 h bins (four points per bin) with every 9th value missing and a 30 h gap (null y). Missing rows must be dropped before binning, never averaged in as zeros, and the gap's EMPTY bins centre to 0 in the lag products while still counting in n.

Double-width tokens (HH mm ss DD MM) need exactly two digits in the JS engine (dayjs strict), so '9:30:00' under HH:mm:ss is blank there. strptime's %H/%M/%S/%d/%m read one OR two digits, so both ports gate each value on the token widths before parsing. Single-width tokens (H m s D M) take one or two digits in all three; see time-unpadded-*.
Onset rule on one 15-min time series (tau 24.5 h). Rows fold at the UTC midnight before the first sample (start 06:30Z).

The onset rule of actogram-rule-onset on a series whose LAST timestamp is missing. The harmonic check filters its candidates by the record span, which was xData[last] - xData[0]; hoursSinceStart keeps the missing time as null and JS reads it as 0, so the span was about 0, no candidate survived and the check returned null (tau NaN). Both ports copied that. The span is now last PRESENT minus first PRESENT time in all three (harmonicCheck.js validEnds).
Offset rule (N 2, M 4, 40th centile) on a NUMBER x axis starting at 3.25 h, with 23.5 h rows.

Two series whose onsets drift across the row boundary (tau 25.5 h forwards past midnight, tau 22.8 h backwards). Series 1 starts a day later, so it folds at series 0's start of day (the shared startTime).
A null gap that empties one row and cuts into its neighbours, plus a spike outside the active phase.
The four lock combinations on one series: fit/fit; fixed tau; fixed theta at reference day 3; both fixed from day 2 (the identity intercept = theta - (tau - P) * refDay).
A rule day range 3..9 scopes the fit; the series unticks day 5 inside it (r1). r2 has the same range and no per-series data.

Series 1 is detached from r1 and carries its own block (fromRule r1, fitWithinRange, tau fixed, own ticks, centile 0 read as 50); series 0 has an unrelated own block that must not fill r1. Series 1 is also detached from r2 with no block, so r2 is all NaN there.

Shipped rest-activity demo (plot 0, two hourly series, 7 days). r1 onset rule; line-only rules fixed at tau 12.3 h (2 tau wins), 47 h (tau/2 wins; 2 tau = 94 h is past half the 167 h record and is filtered out) and 24 h. The harmonicCheck.pin cases.
Shipped split-rhythm demo (plot 51, two hourly series of 26 days, true periods 24.8 and 23.4 h): one onset rule over both series.

Line-only (manual) rules. r1 fits hand-placed points (two in one row: the later wins); on series 1 it has ONE point, so no line (NaN) but n = 1. r2 is fixed at tau 60 h: a line on series 0, but series 1 (2 days) has no harmonic candidate inside its record, so tau is NaN while phi is not. r3 has nothing to fit and nothing fixed: all NaN, n = 0.

An onset rule over a time series and an imported 'bin' column with originTime_ms at 07:30Z. The bin series folds at -rawBinStart0 + (startTime - originTime_ms) / 3.6e6, so its onsets sit at clock hours; the ports used -min(centres), half a bin and 7.5 h off.

Display zone America/New_York: the first sample (03:30Z on 4 March) is 22:30 on 3 March there, so rows fold at New York midnight on 3 March (05:00Z), not at UTC midnight on 4 March. The record crosses the 10 March DST change, which must not move the rows.
^ is right-associative and binds tighter than a unary minus on its left: 2^3^2 = 512, -2^2 = -4, 2^-1 = 0.5; x^2 is a power, not XOR.
log is natural, log10 base 10; log of 0 or a negative is missing (never -Infinity or NaN); Math. aliases and constants.
round() rounds halves toward +infinity like JS Math.round (not banker's): 2.5 -> 3, -2.5 -> -2, 0.49999999999999994 -> 0.
% is the remainder with the sign of the DIVIDEND (C fmod / JS %): -7 % 3 = -1. A zero divisor is missing.
min and max take one or more arguments; a column shorter than the first reads as missing past its end.

fixtures.note: A stored value (#k) is the same scalar in every row.
A stored value that is missing (null) makes every row missing, never 0.
Missing cells (null, blank, whitespace-only, non-numeric text, "NaN", "Infinity") give a missing row; numeric strings use Number() syntax (" 2 ", "1e3", "0x10"); booleans are 1 and 0.
Any step that is not finite is missing from that step on: x/0, sqrt(-1), (-8)^(1/3), exp(1000), 1e999, and min(1/0, 3) is missing rather than 3.
A literal too large for a double (1e999) is missing, and so is every row that uses it.

REFUSED: the Python sandbox escape ().__class__.__base__.__subclasses__() -> os._wrap_close -> os.system (proven to run under the removed eval with empty builtins) is outside the grammar. The node is invalid and writes nothing; the Python port must refuse it without evaluating anything.
REFUSED: a text token that tried to break out of the old JS string-glued expression ("+ ((window.__pwned=1), 0) +") is refused, not run.
REFUSED: a number glued to a name (2x) is an error, not 2*x.
REFUSED: unbalanced parentheses.
REFUSED: Math.pi (wrong case after Math.) and bare names other than pi and e are unknown.
REFUSED: a comma outside a function call.
REFUSED: pow takes exactly two arguments.
REFUSED: a stored-value token whose key does not exist makes the node invalid.
Arithmetic that overflows to Infinity is missing at that step, and stays missing even where a later step would hide it: min(10 * 1e308, 5) is missing, not 5.

Rows with a missing label (null, empty, NaN text) or a missing value (null, blank, whitespace, non-numeric text) are dropped, never read as a group or a zero. Numeric text counts. A whitespace-only label is missing too (isMissingCategory trims).
A group whose mean is not finite (an Infinity value) makes the Welch statistic non-computable: invalid with p NaN, never p = 0.
ANOVA with a non-finite group: F is NaN, so the result is invalid with p NaN.
Zero spread within every group and different means: F is infinite (the emitter cannot record Infinity, so F itself is not compared) and p = 0 is its limit (kept).
Zero spread in both groups and different means: t is infinite (not compared: the emitter records Infinity as null) and p = 0 (kept).

Moving average (simple): rows with a missing x or y (null, blank, whitespace, text) are dropped by the house rule, numeric text counts, rows are sorted by x, and the x output holds only the kept rows.
Moving average (weighted): weight max(0, window - distance) over a centred window (the ports used 1..k ramp weights).
Moving average (exponential): weight exp(-distance / (window / 3)) over a centred window (the ports ran a one-sided EMA). An even window still has floor(window / 2) each side.
Whittaker-Eilers with the JS option names (whittakerLambda, whittakerOrder).
Savitzky-Golay: full windows only; the first and last floor(window/2) points stay as they are.
LOESS: floor(bandwidth * n) nearest points, tricube weights, weighted line.
An unknown smoother type is the moving average with its defaults (window 5, simple).
A time x: smoothing runs on hours since the first time and the x output is written back as epoch ms.

Fill (linear): missing y (null, blank, whitespace, text) is not a known point and is filled between neighbours; the leading and trailing missing rows are outside the known range and stay missing (no extrapolation).
Fill (nearest): a query exactly half-way takes the LOWER neighbour.
Fill (natural cubic spline, Numerical Recipes) - ported to Python and R with this change.
Resample onto start + i*step (makeGrid, no accumulated drift); grid points outside the known x range are missing.
Exactly one known point: only a query at that x has a value (its y); every other row is missing. The ports used to return all-missing below 2 points.
Fill mode with missing x: such a row is not a known point; a row with a present y but a missing x keeps its own y (wave-2 JS rule; Python behaviour).
A time x: the grid is in hours since the earliest time and the x output is written back as epoch ms.
Duplicate x: the LATER value wins as the known point, so a fill row at that x reads the later value (even its own row).
Missing in, missing out (house rule): null, blank, whitespace and text give null, never value + 0 or a concatenated string; numeric text is its value; true is 1; 0x10 is 16 (JS Number syntax).
Missing in, missing out, as Add.
House rule on the fitted rows: a null, blank, whitespace or text y is not fitted (it used to crash the Python port on "") and passes through unchanged; numeric text is fitted as its value.
Sliding standardisation after detrending, using the one-pass JS spread sqrt(E[x^2] - mean^2) over a centred window of floor(window/2) each side.

Rows with a missing predictor (null, blank, whitespace, or the text "nan", which Python float() used to accept as a NaN predictor) are dropped (listwise), never fitted as 0. The fitted/eta/outcome columns are full length with NaN for dropped rows. Reference statsmodels Logit on the complete rows.
fixtures.rToleranceWhy: R fits with glm(binomial), an independent IRLS. On these 18-row fits the standard errors (and so p) differ from the JS by up to ~1e-6 relative while coefficients agree to 1e-9: the convergence limit of two implementations (see tp-logisticregression). Python stays at the default tolerance.

fixtures.note: AR(1) x (phi 0.8) leading y by 3 samples, with missing cells. r(k) = corr(x[t], y[t+k]) stays raw; pvalue is the per-lag p of the PREWHITENED pair (x's Yule-Walker AR filter, order by AIC as R ar(), applied to both); pwR is that prewhitened r.
Scalar extras of the prewhitened cross-correlation: AR order, raw and prewhitened peaks (x leads: positive lag), the smallest per-lag p and its lag, and the Sidak familywise p -expm1(L log1p(-minP)).
Two INDEPENDENT AR(1) series (phi 0.9): the raw correlogram is inflated by autocorrelation; the prewhitened per-lag p and the familywise p are what the node reports.
FFT at the record's OWN length N (240 hourly samples: the 24 h bin is exact), not zero-padded to a power of two. Bins 1 .. below N/2, magnitude 2|X_k|/N.
A run of 2 missing grid slots is filled by linear interpolation (<= 3 in a row and <= 10% of the grid).
Missing VALUES (null, blank) inside the grid are missing slots and are filled the same way.
A run of 5 missing slots is refused (no spectrum), never joined across the gap.
A sample more than a quarter step from its grid slot is off-grid: refused.
Single missing slots that add up to more than 10% of the grid: refused.
An explicit frequency step finer than the record's resolution zero-pads to M = ceil(rate / step); magnitude stays 2|X_k|/N with N the sample count.

A 24.5 h sinusoid in a 250 h hourly record falls between the 25 h and 22.7 h bins; fftPeak refines it by golden-section search on the explained variance of a least-squares sinusoid (centred regressors), reporting its own period and amplitude.
fixtures.toleranceWhy: The refined peak is the argmax of a flat objective (golden-section to 1e-12 of the frequency). V8 Math.cos/sin (fdlibm) and the C library differ by an ulp, which moves the optimum by ~5e-11 in frequency and ~5e-9 relative in phase. Python and R agree with each other to the last digit.

regridUniform: lower-median step, slots, filled count and the filled grid.
regridUniform refusal of a 5-slot run (ok = 0, longestGap 5).
regridUniform refusal of a 5-slot run (ok = 0, longestGap 5).
MovingAnalysis FFT per window: a window that fails the FFT grid check (a 6-sample gap) is NaN, never a spectrum joined across the gap; otherwise the refined fftPeak (period, frequency, magnitude).

fixtures.note: Binned methods start at binOrigin = floor(min(t) / binSize) * binSize, not 0: a record starting at -120 h keeps every sample (it lost all those before 0), and negative times fold by floor, not truncation toward 0.
Hours around 1.7e8 (epoch-sized): binning starts at the first sample's bin, not at 0 (which walked ~1.7e8 empty bins).
Two samples per bin (binSize 2 h on hourly data): the ports now fold the BIN MEANS exactly as binData-then-fold does (they folded raw samples before).
Flat data (ROB-13): Qp is exactly 0 at every fold with the fold's real df, so p = 1 and the threshold is still drawn; not the ratio of two rounding residues.
Per-fold p is the chi-square UPPER tail computed directly (SPEC-14): a strong rhythm has p far below 1e-16, never 1 - CDF = 0.
Missing y (null, blank, whitespace) rows are dropped before binning (valid pairs).
Enright bins from binOrigin too (negative times kept).
Flat data: Enright power 0 at every fold (ROB-13).
Flat data: Lomb-Scargle power exactly 0 everywhere (0.1 is not representable, so the mean-removed residues are ~1e-17 and used to produce a spurious peak).
Lomb-Scargle on valid pairs only (null, blank and whitespace y dropped).
IQR fences on TYPE-7 quartiles (as the Boxplot draws them); missing cells (null, blank, whitespace) stay as they are and numeric text is a value.
z-score rule with zThreshold (population SD); missing cells untouched.
z-score over present values (house rule, numeric text counts); missing cells stay missing.
min-max to [customMin, customMax].
robust: (v - median) / MAD.
unit-vector: v / Euclidean norm.
Degenerate (zero SD): every PRESENT value becomes 0 and missing cells stay missing.
subMatches: numeric compare when both sides are numbers or non-blank numeric strings ("2" and " 2 " match 2).
With find 0, blank and whitespace cells are NOT found (JS == used to replace them), false does not match 0.
A null find matches only missing (null) cells.
FIT-1: a trend with noise and no rhythm. The free period is kept inside [1, 48] h (it used to run to ~2,000 h and fit the ramp with R2 0.97); starts from the least-squares periodogram peaks in range.
A 23.6 h rectangular rhythm with a free period in [20, 28] h; the JS multi-start LM reproduced step for step.
Fixed period (fixedOmega = 2 pi / fixedPeriod).
FIT-2: a 5 / 40 square wave, 12 h active, T fixed at 24. The duration is bounded (t2 = t1 + T sigmoid(u)) so tiles cannot overlap and M stays the rest level instead of drifting to ~-30.
Free period bounded to [20, 28] h with periodogram-peak starts (FIT-1).
FitFunction rectangular model takes minPeriod / maxPeriod (FIT-1).
FitFunction double-logistic model takes minPeriod / maxPeriod (FIT-1).
FIT-3: with a TIME x, persistence is in HOURS (hours since the start): 2 h at 30-min sampling needs 4 consecutive samples (on epoch ms it rounded to one). Crossings are written as a time column.

Consecutive rows more than 1.5x the median spacing apart are a gap: it resets the run like a missing value and does not re-arm: two high samples either side of a 6 h hole (4 in a row by index) are NOT a 1.5 h run.
createSeededRNG (@stdlib minstd-shuffle: Park-Miller with a 32-entry shuffle table and 8 warm-up draws), reproduced bit for bit in Python and R, so the Monte Carlo p-values can be compared.
A negative, fractional seed is truncated and folded into [1, 2^31 - 2] (normalizeSeed).

SurrogateTest p-value (block bootstrap): regridded series, block length round(24 h / step), band-limited largest FFT bin as the statistic, extreme when s >= observed - 1e-9 max(|observed|, |s|). The ports now draw the app's exact sequence.
AR(1) red-noise surrogates (lag-1 alpha clamped to +-0.999, Box-Muller from the seeded RNG).
Shuffle surrogates (Fisher-Yates from the seeded RNG).
Phase-randomised surrogates keep the amplitude spectrum, rhythm included, so the node refuses them for a rhythm test (NaN outputs, invalid).
RhythmicityAnalysis periodogram stat ports: the peak is the largest finite POSITIVE power (spectralPeakIndex; none is NaN, ROB-13).
RhythmicityAnalysis FFT: computeFFT on the series' own grid (no power-of-two padding) and the refined fftPeak as the stat ports.
RhythmicityAnalysis correlogram: the dominant-period peak (first positive lobe).
FitFunction rectangular model with fixOmega and fixedPeriod 12 on a 12 h square wave: the fit runs at 12 h (fixedOmega = 2 pi / fixedPeriod). It used to run at 24 h whatever fixedPeriod said.
